newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIAN EXOTICS -Regional FX ends week on quiet note.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN EXOTICS -Regional FX ends week on quiet note.

text.p: Asian regional currencies ended a calmer week on a quieter note with operators happy to sit on their hands ahead of next week's Thailand economic rescue package.
The one currency which did stand out was the Taiwan dollar which tottered through the five sessions to end at a nine-year low, a 2.8 percent fall on the week.
It managed a brief rally on Friday after news late on Thursday of the central bank's move to raise two key interest rates.
The raising of the rediscount rate to 5.25 percent from 5.00 percent and accomodations against secured loans to 5.625 percent from 5.375 percent helped boost sentiment.
Central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong said the rate hikes were aimed at maintaining stability in the forex market but their effect was short-lived and the Taiwan unit sank towards the close.
It ended at T$28.76 to the U.S. dollar compared with Thursday's close of T$28.70 and last Friday's close of T$27.94.

Apart from the action on the Taiwan, a fairly small market, Asian currencies were basically steady in ranges during the week awaiting news of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) sponsored rescue package for Thailand.
The plan will likely be published next Tuesday and the market has high hopes since it became known the IMF would help put the thing together.
The market reckons the IMF will insist capital controls put in place during the baht crisis are lifted, and traders are looking for IMF credit lines to be established.
There are plenty of disgruntled overseas investors so there is the danger of a large capital outflow when capital controls are lifted, something which would send the baht tumbling anew.
There is also significant room for disappointment should the package not come up to scrach.
"If exchange controls are raised and credit lines are established there might not be that big an outflow," said Chaing Yao Chye, head of Asia Pacific research at CIBC in Singapore.
"But there might be a knee-jerk reaction, which would send the baht down, as some people will want to get out regardless."
The end of the week saw some operators taking profits on long dollar positions but movements this week were unspectacular so profits must have been slim.
The baht itself slipped back a notch after rating agency Standard & Poor's Corp placed Thailand's "A" long-term foreign currency rating on creditwatch.
The onshore baht was at 31.85 to the dollar in late business, down just 0.5 percent on the week. It was still 20 percent down on levels seen before the de facto devaluation on July 2.
The offshore rate ended the week little changed at 32.00.
In Malaysia, the ringgit showed little immediate reaction to news Bank Negara Malaysia asked banks to hold their base lending rates steady.
Banking sources in Kuala Lumpur said the central bank asked them to hold their base lending rates at 9.67 percent despite a recent spike up in interbank rates.
The ringgit was at 2.6285 per dollar after firming through the 2.63 level earlier on dollar profit-taking by funds.
The market was awaiting Malaysia's trade data for June, expected next week, amid talk of a 1.5 billion ringgit deficit after May's surplus of 157 million ringgit.
The Singapore dollar rose through the key 1.47 per dollar level but dealers were looking for the rise to run into resistance around 1.4650.
Trade in the Indonesian rupiah was slow, dominated by covering of short dollar positions for the weekend. Spot rupiah was at 2,612.00 per dollar.

The Philippine peso was firmer as banks scrambled to meet a deadline to cut long dollar positions after the central bank slashed the long dollar limit of banks to five percent of capital from 10 percent, or 10 million, whichever is lower.
Newspapers quoted central bank governor Gabriel Singson as saying he expected banks to unload $200 million due to the new ruling. The peso was at 28.99, a little lower on the week. REUTER
